verse.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy our brother,
to the holy ones and faithful brothers and sisters in Christ at Colossae: Grace to you and peace from God our Father.
verse.note: The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of unusual virtue, whereas the Greek word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God's people.” In this verse the word could also be read as an adjective (“to the holy and faithful brothers and sisters”).

verse.text: We always give thanks to God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you,
since we have heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love you have for all the holy ones
because of the hope stored up for you in the heavens. You heard of this hope before in the word of truth, the good news
verse.note: The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. “Gospel” is now a religious term or the name of a book, so the plain meaning is given here. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

verse.text: that has come to you. Just as it is bearing fruit and growing in all the world, so it has been doing among you too, from the day you heard it and came to know the grace of God in truth.
This is what you learned from Epaphras, our beloved fellow slave, who is a faithful servant of Christ on our behalf
verse.note: The word is built on the ordinary Greek term for a slave, someone owned by a master, and Paul uses it for a co-worker who belongs, as he does, to Christ. Most translations soften it to “fellow servant.” This translation keeps “servant” for a different Greek word, which appears later in this same verse.

Manuscripts are divided between “on our behalf” and “on your behalf”; the two Greek words differ by a single letter and were pronounced alike. The earliest witnesses favor “our,” which presents Epaphras as Paul's representative at Colossae, and the edition translated here adopts it. Many English versions read “your.”

verse.text: and who has also told us of your love in the Spirit.
For this reason we too, from the day we heard it, have not stopped praying for you and asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding,
so that you walk in a way worthy of the Lord, pleasing him in everything: bearing fruit in every good work and growing in the knowledge of God,
being empowered with all power according to the might of his glory, for all endurance and patience, with joy
giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share the lot of the holy ones in the light.
verse.note: The Greek is literally “the share of the lot,” the Septuagint's language for the portions of the promised land assigned to Israel's tribes by lot. Most translations render it “inheritance,” which is the usual English for a related but different Greek word. “Lot” keeps the image of an allotted portion.

verse.text: He rescued us from the authority of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love,
in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation,
verse.note: “Firstborn” can mean first in time or first in rank; in the Septuagint it is used of Israel and of the Davidic king as the one holding the heir's supreme status. Most interpreters take it here as preeminence over creation (hence “firstborn over all creation” in some versions), since the next verse says all things were created in him. Grammatically the phrase could instead place him within creation as its first member, a reading that was at the center of fourth-century controversy.

verse.text: because in him all things were created, in the heavens and on the earth, the visible and the invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. All things have been created through him and for him.
He himself is before all things, and in him all things hold together.
And he himself is the head of the body, the assembly. He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that in everything he himself might come to hold first place,
verse.note: A first-century hearer knew this word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is near-universal in English and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the one Greek word is visible.

verse.text: because in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell

note.term: all the fullness was pleased to dwell
note.traditional: it pleased the Father that in him should all fullness dwell

verse.note: The Greek does not state who was pleased. Either “all the fullness” is the subject, as rendered here, or God is the unstated subject (“God was pleased to have all the fullness dwell in him”). On either reading the fullness is God's own, as 2:9 makes explicit, which is why the sentence continues with “himself” and a masculine “making peace.”

verse.text: and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, [through him] whether the things on the earth or the things in the heavens.
verse.note: The brackets mark words whose place in the original text is doubtful. Some important early manuscripts lack this second “through him”; it may have been dropped as redundant or added by accidental repetition.

verse.text: And you, who were once alienated and hostile in mind, in your evil deeds—
but now you have been reconciled in his body of flesh through his death—to present you holy and unblemished and beyond accusation before him,
verse.note: Most manuscripts and most English versions read “he has now reconciled,” which gives a smooth sentence. The edition translated here follows a few very early witnesses that read “you have been reconciled,” which breaks the grammar and leaves the sentence begun in verse 21 interrupted. The roughness is itself an argument that this is the older reading, since scribes tended to smooth awkward texts, but the question remains disputed.

verse.text: if indeed you remain in the faith, founded and firm, and not shifting from the hope of the good news that you heard, which has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven, and of which I, Paul, became a servant.
Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ for the sake of his body, which is the assembly.

note.term: what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ
note.traditional: that which is behind of the afflictions of Christ

verse.note: The phrase is much debated. Few interpreters think Paul means Christ's death was insufficient, since the chapter has just said it reconciles all things. Common explanations are that “the afflictions of Christ” are the sufferings Christ's people undergo in union with him, or a measure of hardship expected before the end, of which Paul takes his share in carrying the message to the Gentiles.

verse.text: I became its servant according to the stewardship God gave me for you, to make the word of God fully known,
the secret that was hidden for ages and generations—but now it has been revealed to his holy ones.
verse.note: In Jewish Greek of the period this was the ordinary word for a secret, often God's hidden plan that only he can disclose. Most English versions keep “mystery” as an established term, but that word now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, whereas Paul's point is that the secret has been made known. Lexicons give “secret” as a primary gloss.

verse.text: To them God chose to make known how rich among the Gentiles is the glory of this secret, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.
verse.note: The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations” and in the plural regularly refers to the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders it “Gentiles” in that sense and “nations” where peoples as such are in view; it is one word in Greek.

The Greek phrase can mean “in you,” Christ indwelling believers, or “among you,” Christ present and proclaimed among the Gentiles, matching “among the Gentiles” just before, where the Greek uses the same preposition. The traditional “in you” is kept, but many interpreters prefer “among you.”

verse.text: Him we proclaim, admonishing every person and teaching every person in all wisdom, so that we may present every person mature in Christ.
For this I also labor, struggling according to his working that is at work in me with power.
For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those in Laodicea, and for all who have not seen my face in the flesh,
so that their hearts may be encouraged, as they are knit together in love and come to all the riches of the full assurance that understanding brings, to the knowledge of God’s secret, Christ,
verse.note: Most English versions keep “mystery” as an established technical term. In Jewish Greek of the period the word was the ordinary term for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose, and Paul stresses that it has now been made known. “Mystery” today suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, so “secret” is used; the lexicons give it as a primary gloss.

note.traditional: the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ

verse.note: The manuscripts give this phrase in more than a dozen forms, including “of God”, “of God, which is Christ” and the longer wording behind the King James Version. The short and abrupt “of God, of Christ”, found in the earliest witnesses, is generally judged original because it best explains why scribes produced the others. Most interpreters take “Christ” as identifying the secret, as the translation does, though the grammar would also allow “the secret of the God of Christ”.

verse.text: in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.
I say this so that no one may mislead you with plausible arguments.
For even if I am absent in the flesh, I am still with you in spirit, rejoicing as I see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.
So then, just as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him,
rooted and being built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, overflowing with thanksgiving.
See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ.
verse.note: The meaning of this phrase is disputed. In Greek of the period it normally meant the physical elements of which the world is made (earth, water, air, fire); the word could also mean elementary principles, the ABCs of a subject. Many modern versions render “elemental spirits” or “elemental spiritual forces”, taking the elements as personal powers, but clear evidence for that use is later than Paul. The translation keeps the plain term and leaves the question open.

verse.text: For in him all the fullness of deity dwells bodily,
and you have been filled in him, who is the head of every ruler and authority.
In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not done by hands, in the stripping off of the body of flesh, in the circumcision of Christ,
verse.note: The phrase can mean the circumcision that Christ performs or that belongs to him, a spiritual counterpart to the physical rite. It can also mean the circumcision Christ himself underwent, that is, his death, pictured as the stripping off of his body of flesh, in which believers share. The translation leaves both possibilities open.

verse.text: having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.
And when you were dead in your offenses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made you alive together with him. He forgave us all our offenses,
verse.note: The word means a wrongful act against God or another person, and its meaning is not disputed. “Trespass”, the usual rendering, now chiefly suggests entering property without permission, so “offense” is used; the King James Version itself has “offence” for this word in Romans 5.

verse.text: wiping out the record of debt that stood against us with its regulations and was opposed to us; he has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross.
verse.note: The Greek word was the everyday term for a handwritten note acknowledging a debt, signed by the debtor. Ink could be washed or wiped off papyrus, which gives “wiping out” its force. Interpreters differ on whether the “regulations” attached to it are the commandments of the Law of Moses or a more general statement of obligations.

verse.text: He stripped the rulers and the authorities and exposed them publicly, leading them in triumph by the cross.
verse.note: The verb belongs to the same word family as “stripping off” in verse 11. Most modern versions take it to mean that God stripped the powers of their weapons or dignity, hence “disarmed”; the King James Version has “spoiled”. Some interpreters, ancient and modern, take the form to mean “stripped off from himself”, as one throws off a garment. “Stripped” keeps the link with verse 11 and fits the image of captives displayed in a victory parade.

note.term: leading them in triumph by the cross

verse.note: The verb refers to the Roman triumph, the procession in which a victorious general paraded his defeated enemies through the city as a public spectacle. The Greek ends with a pronoun that can mean “in it”, the cross just mentioned, or “in him”, Christ. The translation takes it as the cross and names it for clarity; a good number of versions and scholars prefer “in him”.

verse.text: So do not let anyone judge you over food or drink, or in the matter of a festival, a new moon, or Sabbaths,
which are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.
verse.note: The Greek word is “body”, the same word used throughout this chapter. Shadow and body was a common way of contrasting an outline or foreshadowing with the solid reality that casts it, and “substance” gives that sense. Paul may also intend an echo of the body of Christ, which he mentions in verse 19.

verse.text: Let no one who delights in self-abasement and the worship of angels disqualify you—someone who goes into detail about what he has seen, puffed up without cause by his fleshly mind,
verse.note: The word ordinarily means humility and is a virtue in 3:12. Here and in verse 23 it names something the rival teachers pride themselves on and is linked with harsh treatment of the body, so most scholars think it refers to practices of self-denial such as fasting, for which “humbling oneself” was a regular expression in Jewish Greek. Versions vary among “humility”, “false humility”, “asceticism” and “self-abasement”.

The traditional reading is worship offered to angels. The Greek can equally mean the worship that angels themselves offer, which visionaries claimed to witness or join; Jewish visionary writings of the period show great interest in the heavenly liturgy. Scholars are divided, and the English phrase is left as open as the Greek.

note.term: goes into detail about what he has seen
note.traditional: intruding into those things which he hath not seen

verse.note: This clause is among the most obscure in the letter. The verb can mean to enter, to set foot on, or to investigate in detail, and it is also found in inscriptions for entering a sanctuary after initiation; so the sense may be “which he saw on entering”, referring to visionary experiences. The King James Version follows later manuscripts that add “not” (“things which he hath not seen”); the earliest manuscripts lack it.

verse.text: and does not hold fast to the head, from whom the whole body, supported and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with the growth that comes from God.
If you died with Christ to the elements of the world, why, as though living in the world, do you submit to regulations:

text.q: “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch,”

verse.text: about things that are all destined to perish with use—according to human commands and teachings?
Such things have an appearance of wisdom, with their self-chosen worship, self-abasement, and harsh treatment of the body, but they are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh.

note.term: but they are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh
note.traditional: not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh

verse.note: The Greek of this verse is compressed and its syntax is disputed. The rendering given follows the majority of modern versions: the rules look wise but do nothing to check self-indulgence. Others take it to mean that the rules are of no value and serve only to gratify the flesh, that is, they feed human pride. Either way Paul’s verdict on the regulations is negative.

verse.text: So if you were raised with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
Set your minds on the things above, not on the things on the earth,
for you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
When Christ, your life, is revealed, then you too will be revealed with him in glory.
So put to death the parts of you that are on the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed, which is idolatry.

note.term: the parts of you that are on the earth
note.traditional: your members which are upon the earth

verse.note: The Greek says literally “the members that are on the earth,” where “members” means limbs or body parts. The phrase “on the earth” repeats verse 2, and the list that follows shows that the “limbs” are a figure for the practices the body is used for. Many modern versions paraphrase as “what is earthly in you.”

verse.text: Because of these the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience.
verse.note: Some important early manuscripts lack these words, and some editors think they were added by copyists from the parallel at Ephesians 5:6. SBLGNT prints them as original, and they are translated here. “Sons of disobedience” is a Semitic idiom for people characterized by disobedience.

verse.text: Among them you too once walked, when you were living in these things.
verse.note: The Greek pronoun can be masculine (“among whom,” the disobedient people of verse 6) or neuter (“in which,” the vices of verse 5). With the longer text of verse 6 the reference to people is the more natural one and avoids simply repeating “in these things” at the end of the verse. If the words in verse 6 are not original, the pronoun must refer to the vices.

verse.text: But now you too must lay it all aside: wrath, rage, malice, slander, foul language from your mouth.
Do not lie to one another, since you have stripped off the old self with its practices
verse.note: The Greek is literally “the old human being,” and in verse 10 simply “the new.” Most modern translations render “old self” and “new self,” taking it of the individual’s former and renewed way of being. Some interpreters read it corporately, as the old humanity in Adam and the new humanity in Christ, which suits verse 11, where the “new” is a place in which ethnic and social divisions no longer exist.

verse.text: and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created it,
where there is no Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free, but Christ is all and in all.
verse.note: “Barbarian” was the Greek term for anyone who did not speak Greek and so stood outside Greek culture. Scythians, peoples from north of the Black Sea, were proverbial in the Greek world as the most savage of barbarians. The list moves to the furthest extreme of what a Greek reader considered uncivilized.

verse.text: So, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, put on heartfelt compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience,
verse.note: “Meekness” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a person who is not self-assertive or harsh in dealing with others. “Gentleness” or “humility” is the mainstream modern rendering.

verse.text: bearing with one another and forgiving each other if anyone has a complaint against someone. Just as the Lord forgave you, so you too must forgive.
verse.note: Manuscripts vary here between “the Lord,” “Christ,” and “God.” “The Lord” has strong early support and best explains the others, which look like attempts to specify who is meant. The King James Version follows manuscripts reading “Christ.”

verse.text: And over all these put on love, which is the bond of completeness.
verse.note: The noun means completeness or maturity, the state of having reached the goal, not flawlessness. The phrase can mean the bond that produces completeness, the bond that holds the virtues together as a complete whole, or simply “the perfect bond.” Several modern versions paraphrase along the lines of “which binds everything together in perfect harmony.”

verse.text: And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, the peace to which you were called in one body. And be thankful.
Let the word of Christ dwell among you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with gratitude in your hearts to God.

note.term: teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs

verse.note: The Greek phrases can be grouped in more than one way. “In all wisdom” may go with “dwell” instead of with “teaching,” and the psalms, hymns, and songs may go with “singing” instead of with “teaching and admonishing.” The arrangement here follows the parallels at Colossians 1:28 and Ephesians 5:19. “Among you” could also be “in you,” and “with gratitude” could be “with grace.”

verse.text: And whatever you do, in word or in deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
Husbands, love your wives and do not grow bitter toward them.
Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing in the Lord.
Fathers, do not provoke your children, so that they do not lose heart.
Slaves, obey your human masters in everything, not working only when watched, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord.
verse.note: The Greek is literally “lords according to the flesh.” The word for a slave’s master is the same word translated “Lord” at the end of the verse and in verses 23–24. The passage plays on this throughout, setting the masters of the ordinary human sphere against the one Lord whom slaves and masters alike must answer to.

verse.text: Whatever you do, work at it wholeheartedly, as for the Lord and not for people,
knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are slaves of the Lord Christ.
verse.note: The verse is addressed to slaves, who ordinarily had no right to inherit; inheritance belonged to sons of the household. A first-century hearer would have noticed the reversal in promising slaves an inheritance from the Lord.

note.term: You are slaves of the Lord Christ
note.traditional: for ye serve the Lord Christ

verse.note: The Greek verb form can be a statement (“you serve”) or a command (“serve the Lord Christ”); both are grammatically possible, and translations divide. The verb is from the same root as “slaves” in verse 22, and the rendering here keeps that link visible.

verse.text: For whoever does wrong will be paid back for the wrong done, and there is no favoritism.
Masters, give your slaves what is just and fair, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven.
verse.note: The Greek word for the slave owners (“masters”) is the same word used for Jesus as “Lord.” The verse turns on that identity: those who own slaves are themselves under an owner. “Master” is used here to keep the echo audible.

The Greek noun can mean “equality” or “fairness, equity.” Most interpreters take it here as fair and even-handed treatment, a common sense in the period. A minority argue that Paul is calling for slaves to be treated as equals.

verse.text: Persevere in prayer, keeping alert in it with thanksgiving,
and pray for us as well, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the secret of Christ, for which I am in chains,
verse.note: Most English versions keep “mystery,” treating it as a technical term for a truth once hidden and now revealed. In Jewish Greek of the period the word was the ordinary term for a secret, especially God’s hidden plan that he alone discloses. “Secret” is used here because “mystery” now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, whereas Paul’s point is that this is to be spoken and made plain.

verse.text: so that I may make it plain, as I ought to speak.
Walk in wisdom toward those outside, making the most of the time.

note.term: making the most of the time

verse.note: The verb is a marketplace term meaning to buy up or buy back. Most modern interpreters take it as seizing every opportunity, which is followed here. The older rendering “redeeming the time” assumes the idea of rescuing time from misuse. “Time” here is the word for an opportune moment, not for clock time.

verse.text: Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you know how you ought to answer each person.
Tychicus will tell you all about how things are with me. He is a beloved brother, a faithful servant and a fellow slave in the Lord.
verse.note: Most versions have “fellow servant,” and “servant of Christ” for Epaphras in verse 12. The Greek word in both places is the ordinary term for a slave, the same used for the household slaves addressed in verse 1. A different word, rendered “servant,” stands beside it in this verse. Paul describes himself and his colleagues as owned by the Lord, and “slave” keeps that picture and the distinction between the two words.

verse.text: I am sending him to you for this very purpose, so that you may know how we are and he may encourage your hearts.
verse.note: The Greek verb is in a past tense, written from the viewpoint of the readers, for whom the sending would be past when the letter was read. Tychicus was almost certainly the bearer of the letter, so English idiom calls for the present. Some manuscripts read “that he may know how you are” in place of “that you may know how we are.”

verse.text: He comes with Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you everything that is happening here.
verse.note: This is generally identified with the Onesimus of the letter to Philemon, a slave from a Colossian household who is being sent back. If so, it is notable that Paul introduces him here simply as a faithful and beloved brother and “one of you.”

verse.text: Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, as does Mark, the cousin of Barnabas (you have received instructions about him: if he comes to you, welcome him),
and so does Jesus who is called Justus. Of those from the circumcision, these alone are coworkers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.

note.term: Of those from the circumcision, these alone
note.traditional: who are of the circumcision. These only are my fellow workers

verse.note: “Those from the circumcision” means Jews, here Jewish believers in Christ. The Greek can be punctuated to say either that these three are Jews and are Paul’s only coworkers, or that among his Jewish companions only these three work with him. The second is followed here and by most interpreters, since Paul goes on to name other coworkers who are evidently Gentiles.

verse.text: Epaphras, who is one of you, a slave of Christ, greets you. He is always struggling for you in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God.

note.traditional: perfect and complete / mature and fully assured

verse.note: The first adjective can mean “perfect,” “complete” or “mature”; of persons in Paul it usually means grown-up, fully developed. The participle can mean either “fully convinced” or “filled, made complete.” The first is the more common sense of the verb in Paul and is followed here, while older versions have “complete.”

verse.text: For I testify for him that he toils hard for you and for those in Laodicea and those in Hierapolis.
Luke, the beloved physician, greets you, and so does Demas.
Greet the brothers and sisters in Laodicea, and Nympha and the assembly in her house.

note.term: Nympha and the assembly in her house

verse.note: “Church” is the near-universal rendering. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Greek Scriptures’ term for Israel assembled, whereas “church” now suggests a building or an institution. So “assembly” is used throughout this translation. The manuscripts differ over the name and pronoun: some have the woman Nympha and “her house,” others the man Nymphas and “his house,” and others “their house.” The feminine is followed here, as in most recent editions.

verse.text: And when this letter has been read among you, see that it is also read in the assembly of the Laodiceans, and that you in turn read the one from Laodicea.
verse.note: This is a letter that would reach Colossae by way of Laodicea, a neighboring city about ten miles away. Most scholars think it was a letter of Paul to the Laodiceans that has not survived. Others suggest it was the circular letter now known as Ephesians. The identification is uncertain.

verse.text: And tell Archippus, “See to the service you received in the Lord, so that you fulfill it.”
verse.note: Most versions have “ministry.” The Greek word was an everyday term for service or for a task carried out on someone’s behalf, and did not denote a religious office. “Ministry” now suggests a clerical profession. What Archippus’s task was is not known.

verse.text: The greeting is in my own hand—Paul’s. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.
verse.note: Letters were normally dictated to a secretary. The sender often added a closing line in his own handwriting as a personal touch and a mark of authenticity. Paul does the same at the end of several letters.
